title: What Investment Data Implies about the AI Transition
authors: Jessica A. Wachter, Jonathan D. Wachter
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Revised October 2026 per NBER page.
relevance: Uses firm investment data to size the AI transition. The authors report that five U.S. technology firms account for the majority of AI infrastructure investment, spending $404 billion (2022 dollars) in 2025, with 2026 spending forecast at nearly double that, and they argue these firms risk bankruptcy unless expected profits grow commensurately. A two-sector model with rare productivity booms, calibrated to investment through 2026, implies AI-sector productivity roughly tripled. Simulations with a two-year window and 50% annual chance of a repeat boom imply GDP gains by 2030 of 7% to 53%, with AI shares of GDP of 8% to 36%. The authors attribute the wide range to uncertainty about whether the boom repeats.

title: The AI Buildout and the Economy: Publicly Available Data to Assess AI's Impact
authors: Paul E. Soto, Mason Thieu, Jeffrey S. Allen
institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (FEDS Notes)
verification: Full note read at origin 2026-11-04.
relevance: A Federal Reserve staff note assembling publicly available indicators on AI capabilities and costs, firm investment and adoption, and productivity and labor. The authors conclude the evidence is consistent with a buildout phase rather than the onset of broad-based displacement. AI-related components (software, data centers, power facilities, computer and peripheral equipment) contributed meaningfully to quarterly US GDP growth from 2025 through Q1 2026, though import drags offset much of the gross investment. Census BTOS data show adoption rising with firm size but shallow usage intensity, and early labor-market effects show up more as slower hiring of younger workers than layoffs. A companion XLSX with the underlying series is attached.

title: Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation
authors: Tania Babina, Anastassia Fedyk, Alex He, James Hodson
verification: Abstract read via RePEc listing (ideas.repec.org) 2026-11-04; ScienceDirect publisher page not fetched.
relevance: Peer-reviewed study of firm-level AI investment. The authors build a firm-level AI-investment measure from employee resumes (textual analysis of job profiles) and document a sharp rise in AI investment across sectors. AI-investing firms show higher growth in sales, employment, and market valuations, driven mainly by product innovation rather than process automation. Results hold when instrumenting AI investment with firms' exposure to universities' supply of AI graduates. The authors report that growth benefits concentrate among larger firms and are linked to higher industry concentration, suggesting AI can fuel superstar firms.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
authors: Menaka Hampole, Dimitris Papanikolaou, Lawrence D.W. Schmidt, Bryan Seegmiller
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Revision date September 2025 per NBER page.
relevance: Constructs new task-level measures of workers' exposure to AI using natural language processing, covering 2010-2023 with variation across firms, occupations, and time. Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. A model separates direct substitution from reallocative effects, and an instrument built from historical university hiring networks supports the causal predictions. Overall employment effects are modest: reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms, per the authors.

title: The Labor Market Impact of Digital Technologies
authors: Sangmin Aum, Yongseok Shin
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: Studies Korea, where firms rapidly adopted AI, big data, and IoT. Using regional variation in technology exposure, the authors find significant negative effects on high-skill and female workers, especially in non-IT services, reversing the pattern of earlier waves (the IT revolution and robotization) that mainly hurt low-skill male manufacturing workers. In IT services, high-skill employment declined while high-skill vacancy postings rose, suggesting demand shifted toward newer skills. The authors conclude digital transformation brings both displacement and new opportunities. Korea-focused, useful non-US evidence.

title: The Exposure of Workers to Artificial Intelligence in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
authors: Gabriel Demombynes, Jörg Langbein, Michael Weber
verification: Abstract read at origin (openknowledge.worldbank.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: Applies AI occupational-exposure measures to harmonized labor-force survey microdata from 25 countries covering a population of 3.5 billion people, using detailed 4-digit occupation codes. Within countries, exposure is higher for women, urban workers, and the more educated, but falls with country income: high exposure applies to just 12 percent of workers in low-income countries and 15 percent in lower-middle-income countries, and lack of electricity access limits effective exposure. The authors conclude labor-market impacts of AI in developing countries will likely be more limited than in high-income countries, and that higher exposure signals potential for change rather than inevitable job loss.

title: Buffer or Bottleneck? Employment Exposure to Generative AI and the Digital Divide in Latin America
authors: Paweł Gmyrek, Hernan Winkler, Santiago Garganta
verification: ILO publication page with detailed summary read at origin 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: Joint ILO-World Bank analysis for Latin America and the Caribbean. The authors estimate 26-38% of jobs in the region are exposed to generative AI, with augmentation more likely than automation: 8-14% of jobs could see productivity gains while only 2-5% face potential full automation. Up to half of the jobs that could gain productivity (roughly 17 million, about 7 million held by women) are held back by digital-access gaps. Automation-exposed jobs tend to be urban, formal, higher-paid, and held by women, and in Brazil 8.5% of workers in poverty could benefit versus 14% of those not in poverty. The authors argue low digital inclusion will not buffer automation because most exposed workers already use digital tools.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market in Korea
authors: Stijn Broecke, Carla Ruggiu (OECD); Hyeongjun Bang, Seri No (Korea Labor Institute); with Yongjin Nho and Hwanoong Lee
verification: Foreword, acknowledgements and front matter read from the open OECD PDF 2026-11-04; full 110-page report not read. DOI 10.1787/68ab1a5a-en.
relevance: OECD country review, prepared jointly with the Korea Labor Institute, analyzing AI's impact on Korea's labour market from an internationally comparative perspective and taking stock of Korean policies against the OECD AI Principles. It draws on a KLI worker survey fielded in late February-late March 2025 and an OECD SME survey; per the report and its listing, Korea shows relatively high exposure of jobs to AI, professional occupations benefit from augmentation while clerical support workers face higher displacement risk, and small firms lag in adoption. Offers a policy menu covering skills, social dialogue, social protection and SME support.

title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
authors: Xiang Hui, Oren Reshef, Luofeng Zhou
institution: Organization Science (INFORMS); earlier circulated as CESifo Working Paper 10601
verification: Abstract read via RePEc listing of CESifo WP 10601 (ideas.repec.org) 2026-11-04; INFORMS publisher page returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-04.
relevance: Peer-reviewed study of ChatGPT's release effect on Upwork freelancers. Workers in heavily exposed occupations (e.g., writing, translation) saw declines in both employment and earnings, with similar patterns after image-generating AI tools launched. Past performance and service quality did not shield freelancers; per the authors, top performers appear hit hardest, and generative AI acts as a short-term substitute rather than complement for these knowledge workers. One of the earliest empirical estimates of generative AI's labour-market displacement in gig markets.

title: Now Hiring: Firm-Level Adoption of Generative AI in China
authors: Lixing Li, Zhencen Liu, Anqi Wang, He Wang, Shu Yu
institution: World Bank and Peking University NSD (background paper for World Development Report 2026)
verification: Abstract and introduction read from the PDF 2026-11-04; full 59-page paper not read.
relevance: First comprehensive job-posting-based picture of generative AI adoption among Chinese firms: 72 million job advertisements from China's online recruitment platforms, covering over 5,000 listed and about 2.5 million non-listed firms, 2015-2025, with a keyword classification of three hierarchical GenAI skill categories. By end-2025, 21 percent of listed firms but only 0.2 percent of non-listed firms had recruited GenAI-related roles, with adoption accelerating after the release of DeepSeek-R1. Adoption is higher among larger, more technically sophisticated firms and in market services. The authors discuss limitations of job-posting measures, including missing adoption via off-the-shelf tools.

title: World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence
authors: World Bank
verification: Publication overview page read at origin (worldbank.org) 2026-11-04; full report not read.
relevance: The World Bank's flagship report on AI and development, released August 2026. Its adopt-adapt-advance framework argues developing countries need not build trillion-dollar frontier models but must adapt AI to local languages, institutions and data. The report notes middle-income countries accounted for half of ChatGPT's global traffic within six months of launch, that most workers in developing countries do manual rather than cognitive work so AI initially complements labour, and that a few firms in a handful of economies control frontier models, chips, and data centres, creating dependency risks. It casts governments as enablers, users, and regulators.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence and Productivity: Evidence from firm and worker surveys
authors: Masayuki Morikawa
verification: Abstract read at origin (rieti.go.jp) 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: Japan-focused evidence from original firm and worker surveys. AI-using firms show higher productivity, wages, and medium-term growth expectations, and workers using AI judge their own productivity to have risen by approximately 20 percent on average. More-educated workers are more likely to use AI, implying complementarity between AI and education, and firms expect AI to raise productivity and wages but possibly reduce employment. The author notes reliance on self-reported survey measures as an inherent limitation. Useful Japanese counterpart to US adoption studies.

title: Better Technology, Worse Motivation: Generative Artificial Intelligence's Mediocrity Trap
authors: Yvonne Jie Chen, Jie Gong, Jin Li, Zibo Zhao
institution: Asian Development Bank (Economics Working Paper Series No. 862)
verification: Abstract and front matter read from the open ADB PDF 2026-11-04; full paper not read. DOI 10.22617/WPS260411-2.
relevance: Randomized experiment in which participants completed two illustration tasks with varying access to a text-to-image AI tool; the production process was recorded and outputs evaluated every 15 minutes to trace quality evolution. The authors find AI improves output quality at every point but reduces the returns to continued effort, so many illustrators stop earlier and some submit lower-quality work than they would unaided. For developing economies hoping AI can compensate for scarce skills, they conclude productivity gains may require incentives and work design that sustain effort beyond the good-enough level.

title: AI Readiness and Economic Impacts in Asia and the Pacific (Asian Development Outlook April 2026, Special Topic)
authors: Roshen Fernando, Ed Kieran Reyes
institution: Asian Development Bank (Economic Research and Development Impact Department)
verification: Special topic PDF read at origin 2026-11-04 (opening sections); full ADO volume not read.
relevance: Assesses AI readiness across developing Asia and the Pacific on five dimensions (digital infrastructure, human capital, innovation capacity, institutional strength, economic structure). Advanced Asia-Pacific economies average 0.19 on the digital-infrastructure component of the Artificial Intelligence Preparedness Index while developing economies such as Cambodia, India, Myanmar, Papua New Guinea and the Philippines score below 0.11; the human-capital component averages 0.13 for developing versus 0.17 for advanced economies. The authors argue binding constraints on computing capacity, connectivity and data infrastructure create cascading barriers that keep firm adoption, and hence productivity diffusion, low.

title: Generative AI and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
authors: Lu Fang, Zhe Yuan, Kaifu Zhang, Dante Donati, Miklos Sarvary
institution: Columbia Business School and Zhejiang University (arXiv preprint 2510.12049)
verification: Abstract read at origin (arxiv.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read. v1 submitted 2025-10-14, latest revision June 2026.
relevance: Large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading cross-border online retail platform, which deployed generative AI in seven business workflows (customer service, product matching, advertising, seller services) over 2023-2024. GenAI increased sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3 percent depending on how much the AI added over existing practices; across the four positive applications the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer. Gains come mainly from higher conversion rates rather than larger baskets, with no deterioration in return rates or customer ratings, and larger gains for less experienced consumers and smaller sellers.

title: The effects of generative AI on productivity, innovation and entrepreneurship
authors: Flavio Calvino, Jelmer Reijerink, Lea Samek
verification: Abstract read via RePEc listing (ideas.repec.org) and publication metadata confirmed 2026-11-04; full 59-page PDF not read. DOI 10.1787/b21df222-en.
relevance: OECD synthesis of the experimental evidence (RCTs and field experiments) on how generative AI affects productivity, innovation and entrepreneurship. It finds significant potential to improve firm productivity, especially workers' short-term performance on writing, summarising, editing and coding tasks, with effectiveness depending on the user's experience and the task; human-AI collaboration is described as key to maximising potential. The authors flag research gaps on long-term business effects and on workers' understanding of AI's limitations. Useful as a curated map of the trial evidence base.

title: AI and Productivity in Europe
authors: Florian Misch, Ben Park, Carlo Pizzinelli, Galen Sher
verification: IMF publication page with summary read at origin 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: Simulates AI adoption's medium-term effect on total factor productivity across 31 European countries using Acemoglu's (2024) task-based methodology plus reduced-form adoption predictions. Europe's medium-term gains are around 1 percent cumulatively over five years, above Acemoglu's US estimates but varying widely across scenarios and countries, with substantially larger gains in higher-income countries. In a scenario where AI exposure falls 50 percent in regulated tasks, occupations and sectors, AI-safety and data-privacy rules could reduce Europe's productivity gains by over 30 percent, per the authors.

title: Developments in Artificial Intelligence markets: New indicators based on model characteristics, prices and providers
authors: Christophe André, Manuel Bétin, Peter Gal, Paul Peltier
verification: Abstract read from the open OECD PDF 2026-11-04; the authors' VoxEU/CEPR column summarising the paper was also read the same day.
relevance: Builds new empirical indicators covering generative AI model characteristics, performance and prices, developers, cloud providers, and downstream applications globally over two years. The abstract concludes that trends are indicative of dynamism for the time being, including declining quality-adjusted prices and a growing number of market players and model offerings, but that risks remain from bottlenecks in key AI inputs, notably data, computing power and skills. The companion column by the authors reports GPT-4-level access roughly 1,000 times cheaper than in March 2023 and a frontier that is oligopolistic but highly contestable, with five to six players alternating at the frontier.

title: Concentrating Intelligence: Scaling and Market Structure in Artificial Intelligence
authors: Anton Korinek, Jai Vipra
institution: Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET Working Paper No. 228)
verification: Abstract and introduction read from the PDF 2026-11-04; full paper not read. DOI 10.36687/inetwp228.
relevance: Analyzes the cost structure of foundation models (LLMs), emphasizing computational resources, data, and talent, and identifies significant economies of scale and scope that may create a tendency toward greater market concentration. The authors explore two competition concerns, the risk of market tipping and the implications of vertical integration, and derive policy remedies to maintain a competitive landscape. Revised version of a paper presented at the 79th Economic Policy panel meeting (April 2024, Brussels); an earlier version circulated as Market Concentration Implications of Foundation Models.

title: Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises (Statistics Explained)
authors: Eurostat
verification: Statistics read at origin 2026-11-04 (article extracted December 2025); underlying dataset isoc_eb_ai not downloaded.
relevance: Official EU enterprise-survey statistics on AI use, usable to benchmark adoption claims. 19.95 percent of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees used AI technologies in 2025, up 6.47 percentage points from 13.48 percent in 2024. By size class in 2025: 17 percent of small, 30.36 percent of medium, and 55.03 percent of large enterprises. Denmark is highest (42.03 percent) and Romania lowest (5.21 percent); 26 EU countries saw increases over 2024. The article notes figures follow the ISOC survey module and are updated annually.

title: AI Unboxed and Jobs: A Novel Measure and Firm-Level Evidence from Three Countries
authors: Erik Engberg, Holger Görg, Magnus Lodefalk, Farrukh Javed, Martin Längkvist, Natália Pimenta Monteiro, Hildegunn Kyvik Nordås, Giuseppe Pulito, Sarah Schroeder, Aili Tang
verification: Abstract read via RePEc listing (ideas.repec.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: A measurement paper for AI-exposure research. The authors build a time-variant occupational exposure measure based on AI capabilities data and occupational work content, broken down by AI subdomains such as language and image modelling, and validate it on near-universal register data on firms and workers from Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden covering about two decades. White-collar occupations face the greatest exposure, especially those with little social interaction. Firm-level labour-demand estimates show exposure positively linked to demand for high-skilled white-collar workers and negatively for blue-collar workers, an upskilling effect, with heterogeneous effects across AI subdomains.
